Revised question

Which frame equations are intrinsic geometric identities, and how do they change on a curved manifold?

The historical Beta-frame equations reproduce the Frenet–Serret system under an arc-length and positive-curvature hypothesis. They describe local rotation of an orthonormal moving frame; their coefficients are not automatically new physical tensor components.

Definitions and assumptions

Let γ(s) be a C³ unit-speed curve in oriented Euclidean three-space with curvature κ=||γ″||>0.

Set T=γ′, N=T′/κ, B=T×N, and τ=−B′·N.

Frenet–Serret equations and the Darboux vector

T′=κN, N′=−κT+τB, B′=−τN. The vector Ω=τT+κB satisfies E′=Ω×E for E=T,N,B.

Derivation or proof

Because the frame is orthonormal, differentiating its pairwise dot products makes its derivative matrix skew-symmetric. The definition gives T′=κN and therefore N′·T=−κ. Since T′·B=0 and B′·T=−B·T′=0, B′ lies along N; its coefficient is −τ. Orthogonality then gives N′·B=τ and no N-component, proving all three equations. Cross products T×N=B, B×T=N and T×B=−N verify the Darboux expression. On an oriented Riemannian three-manifold, replace ordinary derivatives by ∇_T and use the metric-compatible cross product; covariant frame equations still describe motion along the curve. Ambient curvature enters comparisons around loops and commutators of covariant derivatives, not an arbitrary extra term in each Euclidean formula.

Worked example

Take γ(s)=(a cos(s/c),a sin(s/c),bs/c) with c=√(a²+b²) and a>0.

Its speed is one, κ=a/(a²+b²), and τ=b/(a²+b²). For a=b=1 these are both 1/2. A planar circle has b=0, hence τ=0 and a fixed binormal; a straight line has κ=0 and the Frenet normal is undefined, requiring a different frame such as a parallel-transport frame.

The equations have exact hypotheses, a geometric derivation, and a worked nonplanar example.

At zero curvature, the Frenet construction fails even for a smooth curve. A frame equation by itself supplies no field equation, stress tensor, or unification with quantum groups.

How do curvature forms yield topological numbers, and why must they not be confused with a variational gravitational action?

The recovered catalogue mentioned Pontryagin terms alongside curvature actions. Chern–Weil theory gives precise invariant integrals; their local variations are boundary terms under the appropriate hypotheses. This is a different role from an Einstein–Hilbert kinetic term.

For a connection A on a complex bundle, F=dA+A∧A and D_AF=0 is the Bianchi identity.

For a Hermitian line bundle write its unitary curvature as iF_real with F_real a real two-form; c₁ is represented by F_real/(2π).

On the unit four-torus, a line bundle with curvature 2π(n dx₁∧dx₂+m dx₃∧dx₄) has ∫c₁²=2nm. In general δ tr(F∧F)=2d tr(δA∧F).

For the line-bundle example, squaring the two-form gives twice the cross term because two-forms commute under wedge product and each individual square vanishes. Integration over the unit oriented four-torus gives 2nm. Integer periods of the normalized curvature encode the line bundle’s Chern class. For the variation, δF=D_AδA. Cyclicity of trace and the even degree of F give δtr(F∧F)=2tr(D_AδA∧F). Apply the covariant Leibniz rule and use D_AF=0; taking a trace removes commutators, leaving an ordinary exterior derivative. On a closed manifold its integral is zero by Stokes, so a constant multiple of this topological term contributes no local bulk Euler–Lagrange equation under smooth variations within the same bundle.

Choose n=2,m=3. Compare a closed torus with a four-manifold with boundary.

The integral is 2·2·3=12. For the underlying oriented real plane bundle, p₁=c₁² in this convention, so its first Pontryagin number is also 12. On a manifold with boundary, the action variation is the boundary integral 2∫∂M tr(δA∧F), which need not vanish without boundary conditions or a compensating term.

A topological curvature integral is invariant under allowed interior deformations, while boundary data can carry genuine variation.

Revised question

Which hypotheses turn a formal differential equation into a uniquely solvable weak problem?

The recovered mathematical-physics catalogue included weak formulations and Lax–Milgram. A complete one-dimensional example gives a concrete existence, uniqueness, and stability result, while exposing the difference between coercivity and a merely symmetric expression.

Definitions and assumptions

Let H=H₀¹(0,1) with norm ||u||_H=||u′||₂.

For μ≥0 define a(u,v)=∫u′v′+μ∫uv and ℓ(v)=∫fv for f∈L².

Unique weak solution and an energy bound

There exists a unique u∈H satisfying a(u,v)=ℓ(v) for every v∈H, and ||u′||₂≤||f||₂/π. If μ=0 and f=1, the solution is u(x)=x(1−x)/2.

Derivation or proof

Poincaré’s inequality ||v||₂≤||v′||₂/π makes ℓ bounded with norm at most ||f||₂/π. Cauchy–Schwarz and the same inequality show a is bounded. Since μ≥0, a(v,v)≥||v′||², so it is coercive. To prove the needed existence rather than merely name it, equip H with the equivalent inner product a. The Riesz representation theorem supplies u with a(u,v)=ℓ(v). Uniqueness follows because a(u−w,u−w)=0 implies u=w. Taking v=u and combining coercivity with the functional bound gives the stated estimate. For f=1,μ=0, differentiating x(1−x)/2 gives −u″=1 and zero endpoint values; integration by parts verifies the weak equation.

Worked example

Compare μ=0 with the sign-changed form a_−(u,v)=∫u′v′−π²∫uv.

The function sin(πx) is nonzero but a_−(sinπx,v)=0 for every v∈H by integration by parts. Thus the sign-changed form is not coercive and its homogeneous equation is nonunique. The original solution has u′=(1−2x)/2 and ||u′||₂²=1/12, consistent with the bound ||u′||₂≤1/π.

Existence follows from explicit Hilbert-space hypotheses, and the counterexample identifies exactly where uniqueness can fail.

Scope

This is a linear elliptic result, not a general theorem for nonlinear quantum or gravitational equations. Boundary conditions and coefficient lower bounds are essential.

Further development

For a finite element approximation, use Galerkin orthogonality and coercivity to derive a best-approximation error estimate in the energy norm.

Revised question

Which conclusions about a running parameter follow from its stated differential equation, without adding an unconstructed field theory?

The historical catalogue invoked renormalization-group flow and scale hierarchies. Once a beta function and convention are fixed, its local consequences are an ordinary differential equation. The integration is exact within that assumed truncation, while physical validity remains a separate question.

Definitions and assumptions

Let t=log(μ/μ₀) and consider dg/dt=−b g² with b a fixed real number.

A fixed point is a zero of the specified beta function β(g); a truncation is a chosen approximate beta function, not an exact model by default.

Exact solution of the quadratic beta-flow model

For initial g(0)=g₀, g(t)=g₀/(1+bg₀t) on the maximal interval where the denominator is nonzero. For b,g₀>0 it decreases to zero as t→+∞ and has a backward pole at t=−1/(bg₀).

Derivation or proof

If g₀=0 the zero solution is immediate. Otherwise differentiating 1/g gives d(1/g)/dt=b as long as g is nonzero. Integration gives 1/g=1/g₀+bt and hence the formula; direct substitution verifies it. Local uniqueness for the polynomial vector field prevents a nonzero solution from crossing the zero equilibrium. The denominator determines the maximal interval in this model. A pole of a truncated equation does not by itself prove a physical singularity: neglected terms or a different effective description can become important first. Replacing μ by a different dimensional unit leaves t unchanged if μ and μ₀ use the same unit; writing log μ alone would hide a necessary reference scale.

Worked example

Take b=2,g₀=1/4 and compare scales μ₀ and e²μ₀.

At t=2 the coupling is (1/4)/(1+1)=1/8. The model’s backward pole is at t=−2, corresponding to μ=μ₀e^(−2). If β(g)=−2g²+cg³ instead, the extra term changes the ODE and may add a nonzero fixed point at 2/c; it is not legitimate to retain the old solution without an error estimate.

The recovered scaling language becomes a checkable flow calculation with a defined reference scale and a stated approximation.

Scope

No interacting continuum quantum field theory is constructed. Numerical coefficients depend on the coupling definition and loop convention, so the example is not a numerical QCD prediction.

Further development

For a beta function known with a remainder bound, compare the exact and truncated flows by a differential inequality on a compact coupling interval.

Revised question

What does sphere eversion allow, and what does the Willmore energy of a spherical immersion actually bound?

The historical geometry discussion combined sphere eversion, Boy and Morin surfaces, and bending energy. Regular homotopy permits self-intersections but keeps the differential injective. This distinction is essential: an eversion is not a deformation through embedded spheres.

Definitions and assumptions

An immersion f:S²→R³ has rank-two differential everywhere; an embedding is additionally injective with the subspace topology.

Use H=(κ₁+κ₂)/2 and W(f)=∫H²dA, where κ₁,κ₂ are principal curvatures.

Spherical Willmore inequality

Every smooth immersion of S² into R³ satisfies W≥4π. A round sphere has W=4π independently of its radius.

Derivation or proof

Pointwise H²−K=((κ₁−κ₂)²)/4≥0, where K=κ₁κ₂ is Gaussian curvature. Integrating and applying Gauss–Bonnet to the intrinsic metric on the parameter sphere yields ∫K dA=2πχ(S²)=4π, even if the image self-intersects. Therefore W=4π+(1/4)∫(κ₁−κ₂)²dA≥4π. Equality forces the surface to be umbilic everywhere; the bound itself needs only the displayed identity. For a round radius-R sphere, H=±1/R and area=4πR², so W=4π. Scaling all lengths by c changes H² by c^(−2) and area by c², proving scale invariance. The existence of sphere eversion is a separate regular-homotopy theorem and is not proved by this energy inequality.

Worked example

Compare a round sphere at radii one and three, and distinguish the parameter sphere from an immersed projective plane such as Boy’s surface.

The energies are 1·4π=4π and (1/9)·36π=4π. In a regular homotopy the oriented normal may reverse relative to the original parametrization while the differential remains rank two; intermediate self-intersections are allowed. A projective plane has different topology from S², so its Gauss–Bonnet integral is 2π rather than 4π and the spherical proof must not be copied without changing the Euler characteristic.

The energy convention, topology, and admissible class of deformations are explicit, preventing a factor-of-four normalization error or an embedding claim.

Scope

The pointwise estimate alone does not describe an optimal eversion path or its maximal bending energy. Singular pinches are not immersions and are excluded.

Further development

Track the differential rank and self-intersection set along an explicitly specified immersion family, then study its maximum Willmore energy as a separate variational problem.

Revised question

How do transverse and traceless constraints reduce a plane-wave symmetric tensor to two independent components?

The recovered TT conditions are linear constraints on a spatial symmetric perturbation after choosing a propagation direction and gauge. Their two-dimensional solution space can be computed directly without asserting a nonlinear quantum-gravity construction.

Definitions and assumptions

Let h be a symmetric 3×3 matrix representing the spatial amplitude of a plane wave with nonzero wavevector k.

The transverse condition is k_i h_ij=0 and the trace condition is Σ_i h_ii=0.

TT amplitude space for a fixed direction

For k parallel to the z-axis, every TT amplitude is h=h₊[[1,0,0],[0,−1,0],[0,0,0]]+h×[[0,1,0],[1,0,0],[0,0,0]]. Under a transverse basis rotation by φ, the two components mix by a rotation of angle 2φ.

Derivation or proof

Symmetry begins with six independent entries. Since k_z≠0, transversality forces h_zx=h_zy=h_zz=0. The trace then gives h_yy=−h_xx, leaving h_xx and h_xy as the two free entries. Write the transverse 2×2 matrix as [[a,b],[b,−a]] and transform it by R(φ)^T h R(φ). Multiplication gives a′=a cos2φ+b sin2φ and b′=−a sin2φ+b cos2φ for that passive convention. This double-angle transformation explains the spin-two polarization behavior at the level of the linear representation. The Frobenius squared norm is 2(a²+b²) for real amplitudes and is invariant under the basis change.

Worked example

Take h₊=1,h×=0 and rotate the transverse axes by φ=π/4.

cos(π/2)=0 and sin(π/2)=1, so the new components are (0,−1) in the stated passive convention. The original plus pattern becomes a cross pattern of the same norm; a rotation by π returns the same tensor components, while a rotation by π/2 changes both signs.

The two polarization degrees of freedom and their transformation law follow from explicit linear constraints.

Scope

The calculation assumes a fixed nonzero wavevector and a linearized plane-wave setting. Gauge fixing, the linearized field equation, and nonlinear gravitational dynamics are additional questions. A generic symmetric tensor field is not automatically TT.

Further development

For any nonzero k, form P=I−kk^T/||k||² and the projector h↦PhP−(1/2)P tr(Ph), then verify transversality, tracelessness, and idempotence.

Revised question

How should Jordan structure be certified exactly, and when can symmetry help compute it?

The recovered code proposal mixed Jordan decomposition with space-group operations. Similarity preserves Jordan form; an unrelated geometric symmetry does not improve it. Nullity increments supply exact certificates, while a simple perturbation explains the instability of numerical Jordan decisions.

Definitions and assumptions

For an eigenvalue λ let d_k=dim ker(A−λI)^k, with d₀=0.

A commuting symmetry U satisfies AU=UA and therefore preserves every generalized eigenspace.

Jordan block counts from nullities

The number of Jordan blocks for λ of size at least k is d_k−d_{k−1}; the number of blocks of size exactly k is 2d_k−d_{k−1}−d_{k+1}.

Derivation or proof

On a Jordan block of size s, the k-th power of its nilpotent part has nullity min(k,s). Its successive increment is one precisely when s≥k. Summing over blocks gives the first formula, and subtracting consecutive increments gives the second. This argument is exact and does not choose a tolerance. If U commutes with A, then U commutes with every power of A−λI and maps its kernel into itself, so known symmetry sectors can reduce the computation. A generic change of coordinates S only conjugates A to S^(−1)AS and cannot alter the block sizes. Numerical singular-value thresholds estimate approximate nullities; they do not turn a near-defective matrix into a certified exact Jordan form.

Worked example

Take the recovered A=[[5,4,2],[0,1,0],[0,0,3]], and compare N_ε=[[0,1],[ε,0]].

A has distinct eigenvalues 5,1,3 and eigenvectors (1,0,0), (−1,1,0), (−1,0,1), so it is diagonalizable. For ε=0, N_ε has one size-two nilpotent block. For every nonzero ε it has two distinct complex eigenvalues ±√ε and is diagonalizable. An arbitrarily small perturbation changes the exact Jordan structure.

The matrix example needs no generalized eigenvector, and exact nullity formulas provide a reproducible standard for code verification.

For the determinant assertion, a diagonal matrix’s determinant is the product of its diagonal entries, immediately yielding f. Revised question

Which algebraic conditions define a projection, and why do negative eigenvalue real parts not prove monotone norm decay?

The historical framework listed P†=P, P²=P, and eigenvalue real parts ≤0 near the same operator discussion. These are distinct properties. Orthogonal projections have a very restricted spectrum; stable generators require an evolution equation and a norm estimate.

Definitions and assumptions

An orthogonal projection satisfies P*=P and P²=P.

For u′=Au, Euclidean energy decreases for all initial data exactly when A+A* is negative semidefinite.

Projection spectrum and the dissipativity criterion

An orthogonal projection has eigenvalues only zero and one. The semigroup exp(tA) is norm-contracting for every t≥0 if A+A*≤0; eigenvalues with negative real parts alone do not imply this contraction.

Derivation or proof

If Pv=λv then λ²v=λv, so λ∈{0,1}. Self-adjointness ensures an orthonormal eigenbasis and ||P||≤1. For an evolving vector, d||u||²/dt=⟨u,(A+A*)u⟩, proving sufficiency of the dissipativity condition. If energy is nonincreasing for every initial vector, evaluating the derivative at t=0 proves necessity. A matrix may nevertheless have all eigenvalues in the left half-plane and have a positive symmetric part because its eigenvectors are nonorthogonal. Such a matrix eventually decays in finite dimensions but may initially amplify vectors. This is a norm-sensitive phenomenon rather than a contradiction of spectral stability.

Worked example

Take A=[[-1,4],[0,−1]] and u(0)=(1,1).

Both eigenvalues equal −1. Yet A+A*=[[-2,4],[4,−2]] has eigenvalues 2 and −6, and the initial energy derivative is (1,1)(A+A*)(1,1)^T=4>0. The exact solution is e^(−t)(1+4t,1), confirming transient amplification. By contrast −P generates exp(−tP)=I−P+e^(−t)P, a contraction that preserves the kernel component.

Projection, asymptotic spectral stability, and monotone energy stability are mathematically different and can be checked separately.

Scope

This is finite-dimensional analysis. For unbounded generators, the operator domain and semigroup generation theorem are essential; a formal spectrum alone is even less sufficient.

When do odd generators define a cohomological differential, and what extra checks are needed for a proposed superalgebra deformation?

Definitions and assumptions

For homogeneous elements, [x,y]=xy−(−1)^{|x||y|}yx is the graded commutator.

Take an odd Q and an even central H with [Q,Q]=2H and [H,Q]=0.

Adjoint differential and its square

For d(x)=[Q,x], the graded Jacobi identity gives d²(x)=[H,x]. Hence d²=0 when H is central, or after restricting to elements commuting with H.

Derivation or proof

Apply graded Jacobi to Q,Q,x. Since Q is odd, the two terms with nested Q brackets agree and yield 2[Q,[Q,x]]=[[Q,Q],x]. Substituting [Q,Q]=2H gives d²=[H,·]. If H is central the right side vanishes, defining cohomology ker d/im d because im d⊆ker d. The one-even, one-odd bracket table itself satisfies graded Jacobi: the only possibly nontrivial all-Q triple reduces to [Q,H]=0. For a proposed deformation [x,y]_ε=[x,y]+εφ(x,y)+O(ε²), the first-order Jacobi coefficient must vanish; this is the 2-cocycle condition. At the next order, the quadratic obstruction is a 3-cocycle, so an H² class is an infinitesimal deformation and need not extend to an exact one.

Q²=I, so [Q,Q]=2I and H is central. For an even diagonal X=diag(a,b), dX=[[0,b−a],[a−b,0]], an odd matrix; applying d again gives Q(dX)+(dX)Q=0. This directly checks d²=0. By contrast two exterior-algebra generators θ₁,θ₂ satisfy θ₁θ₂+θ₂θ₁=0, not an arbitrary scalar C₁₂.

Definitions and assumptions

For a polynomial over Q, its splitting field is the smallest field containing all roots; its Galois group consists of Q-automorphisms.

For Q(i), complex conjugation is the nontrivial automorphism, and unramified odd primes split or remain inert.

For an odd prime p, x²+1 has a root in F_p exactly when p≡1 mod4. Thus p splits in Q(i) for p≡1 mod4 and is inert for p≡3 mod4; p=2 is ramified.

If a²=−1 mod p, Fermat’s theorem gives 1=a^(p−1)=(−1)^((p−1)/2), so p≡1 mod4. Conversely the finite multiplicative group F_p× is cyclic. If p≡1 mod4 and g generates it, a=g^((p−1)/4) has square g^((p−1)/2)=−1, the unique element of order two. The factorization of x²+1 into distinct linear factors or an irreducible quadratic modulo odd p gives the corresponding prime splitting in the Gaussian integers. At p=2, 2=−i(1+i)², so the prime ramifies. This computes local behavior from one global field; it does not prove a general reciprocity or Langlands theorem.

Five-periodic A₂ exchange sequence

Then x₆=(1+x₅)/x₄ simplifies to x, and x₇=(1+x₆)/x₅ simplifies to y. Since the recurrence is deterministic in the rational function field, the pair repeats and proves the entire five-periodicity. What does a quiver Grassmannian parameterize, and how do its coefficients depend on the actual arrow map?

The recovered quiver discussion assigned subrepresentation coefficients to quantum pathways without specifying a representation. Even the smallest nontrivial arrow shows that dimensions alone do not determine the variety: the arrow map changes the parameter space and its Euler characteristic.

For the quiver1→2 take vector spaces V₁=C²,V₂=C and arrow f:V₁→V₂.

A subrepresentation of dimension vector(1,0) consists of a line U⊂C² and the zero subspace in C with f(U)=0.

Exact quiver Grassmannian and Euler count

If f has rank one, Gr_(1,0)(V) is a single point and has Euler characteristic1. If f=0, it is P¹(C) and has Euler characteristic2.

Derivation or proof

The subrepresentation condition is precisely U⊂ker f. For rank-one f, the kernel is one-dimensional, so the only eligible line is ker f itself. For f=0, every line is eligible, giving the ordinary Grassmannian Gr(1,2)=P¹. Its usual affine-cell decomposition is C together with one point at infinity; their compactly supported Euler characteristics are1 and1, giving2, which agrees with its ordinary Euler characteristic as a compact sphere. In coordinates f(z₁,z₂)=z₁, a line[z₁:z₂] qualifies exactly when z₁=0, giving the point[0:1]. This exhibits a proper algebraic subset of the ambient Grassmannian cut out by the arrow compatibility equation.

Worked example

Compare the same dimension vector(2,1) for f=(1,0) and f=(0,0).

The vector-space dimensions are identical, but the Euler coefficient for subdimension(1,0) changes from1 to2. At subdimension(1,1), the target subspace is all C, so every source line qualifies for either map and the variety is P¹ with Euler characteristic2. Thus every coefficient must specify both the subdimension and the arrow representation.

What survives rigorously from the recovered F₁ and hyperfield analogies?

The recovered discussion treated F₁ points, Euler characteristics, and hyperfield inverses as quantum-state concepts. The basic arithmetic is precise but different from field arithmetic. F₁ is not an ordinary one-element field; the Krasner hyperfield uses set-valued addition.

Definitions and assumptions

The Krasner hyperfield K={0,1} has ordinary multiplication,0 as additive identity,and1⊞1={0,1}.

For a finite field F_q, P¹(F_q) is the set of one-dimensional subspaces of F_q².

F_q² hasq²−1 nonzero vectors and each line containsq−1 of them, so the quotient count is(q²−1)/(q−1)=q+1. P¹(C) has one0-cell and one real2-cell, giving Euler characteristic2. This explains a common counting heuristic atq=1; it does not create a field with one element. For the hyperfield quotient, nonzero a and b can sum to zero by choosing b=−a. They can also sum to a nonzero element when the field has at least three elements, with an appropriate nonzero pair. Thus the sum of the single nonzero equivalence class with itself contains both0 and1. Multiplication remains well-defined and1^(−1)=1, but addition is not an ordinary single-valued operation.

Compare ordinaryF₂ with the Krasner hyperfield.

InF₂,1+1=0 only. InK,1⊞1={0,1}. ThereforeK is not simplyF₂ with a different name. A nonzero hyperfield element has a multiplicative inverse, but this does not mean a vector state has a second configuration or that a linear operator has an inverse. The objects and operations have different types.

The recovered F₁ intuition is grounded in an exact polynomial count and a clearly defined hyperoperation.

Revised question

What does the standard toric code prove about local errors, and what would a proposed extension have to improve?

The historical claim of going beyond toric code needs a baseline with a defined lattice, code space, and error model. The square torus code has exact commuting stabilizers and nonlocal logical operators; these properties can be proved at the Pauli-algebra level.

Definitions and assumptions

Place one qubit on every edge of an L×L square lattice with periodic boundaries,L≥3.

For a vertexv setA_v=∏_{e incident v}X_e; for a plaquettep setB_p=∏_{e∈∂p}Z_e.

Commuting stabilizers and distanceL

AllA_v andB_p commute. Their common+1eigenspace encodes two qubits, and a shortest noncontractible Pauli loop has lengthL, giving code distanceL.

Derivation or proof

X andZ anticommute on one edge. A star and plaquette share either zero or two edges, so their commutation sign is(+1)or(−1)²=+1. Products of all stars and all plaquettes each equalI because every edge occurs twice. On the connected torus these are the only independent relations of each type; thus the stabilizer rank is2L²−2 among2L²qubits and the code dimension is2². AZ string anticommutes with stars at its endpoints, detecting open-string errors; a closed string commutes with all stars. Contractible loops are products of plaquettes and act trivially on the code. A noncontractible loop cannot be such a boundary and acts logically. The shortest noncontractible direct or dual cycle hasLedges, yielding the minimum nontrivial logical Pauli weightL.

Worked example

TakeL=3 and follow a Z string along one periodic row.

There are18edge qubits,9stars,and9plaquettes,with16independent stabilizers and a four-dimensional code space. A one-edgeZerror creates two violated star syndromes; a length-three wrappedZloop has no syndrome but changes a logical state. Thus local detectability and logical vulnerability coexist exactly as the distance statement predicts.

The baseline protection is a precise code-space statement against bounded-weight Pauli errors, not an unrestricted immunity claim.

Scope

This does not prove passive self-correction at nonzero temperature, nor protection against arbitrary correlated errors. The MPPF proposal had no recovered code, stabilizers, or distance certificate with which to establish an improvement.

Further development

For a claimed extension, provide its commuting constraints or alternative code definition, count independent logical degrees of freedom, and exhibit both a lower bound and a matching logical operator for its distance.
